title: CI/CD Platform
description: Describe a build once and run it in the same container on your laptop and in any CI, with deploys kept in CI. The whole picture, then a guide to build your own.

headline: CI/CD
Platform
hero.lead: Describe a build once, in the project. It runs in the same container on your laptop and in any CI, and deploys stay in CI. Below: the whole picture, then a guide to build your own.

picture.title: The whole picture.
body: A registry holds tool images. A shared Taskfile knows how to run them. Each project names its work. Your laptop and any CI call those names and get the same box. Delivery waits behind a gate, for CI only.

headline: The guide
guide.title: The guide: build your own
guide.intro: The steps go in build order. Each one ends with a check you can run before moving on.

needs.title: Before you start
items: Docker and Task on your machine
A container registry you can push to
A git repository for shared Taskfiles
Any CI whose runners can start containers

steps.title: Pack the tools
steps.why: Every tool a project needs lives in an image, at a pinned version. Nobody installs a toolchain by hand.
actions: Write a Dockerfile per tool and keep the versions it takes next to it.
Build it for every platform your laptops and runners use.
Push it to your registry under a version tag. Skip `latest`.

code.label: Build and publish
code.code:
docker buildx build --platform linux/amd64,linux/arm64 \
  --build-arg NODE_VERSION=22 \
  --tag your-registry/node:22 --push tools/node

steps.check: `docker run --rm your-registry/node:22 node --version` prints the version you pinned.
steps.tip: Rebuild on a schedule to pick up patches. Pin a digest when you need the exact bytes.

steps.title: Teach the run
steps.why: One shared Taskfile knows how to start each tool's container. Projects call it instead of copying `docker run` lines.
actions: Create a repository for shared Taskfiles, one file per tool.
Add a task that runs a command in the tool's image, with the project mounted and the cache kept on the host.
Lock the container down: drop capabilities, forbid new privileges, run as the host user.
Tag a release. Projects will pin its commit.

code.label: shared-tasks/node/Taskfile.yml
code.code:
version: '3'

tasks:
  exec:
    cmds:
      - docker run --rm --init --cap-drop ALL
          --security-opt no-new-privileges
          --user "$(id -u):$(id -g)"
          --volume "{{.ROOT_DIR}}:/workspace"
          --volume "{{.ROOT_DIR}}/.cache/node:/tmp/cache"
          --workdir /workspace
          your-registry/node:{{.NODE_VERSION | default "22"}}
          sh -c '{{.CMD}}'

rows.note: The container goes away after the run.
Your project is mounted, not copied.
The cache stays on your disk between runs.
Files come out yours, not root's.

steps.check: `task --taskfile shared-tasks/node/Taskfile.yml exec CMD='node --version'` prints the version from inside the container, and no root-owned files appear.

steps.title: Name the work
steps.why: The project owns the names CI will call and what they do. The name is the contract. The steps behind it are yours.
actions: Include the shared Taskfile, pinned to a commit.
Declare a `ci/<area>/<verb>` task for everything CI should run: build, test, lint.
Change the steps behind a name whenever you like. Keep the name.

code.label: Taskfile.yml, in the project
code.code:
version: '3'

includes:
  node: https://your-git/shared-tasks/raw/<commit>/node/Taskfile.yml

tasks:
  ci/node/build:
    cmds:
      - task: node:exec
        vars: { CMD: npm ci && npm run build }

steps.tip: Shared templates can bring ready jobs. A project uses one as it is, overrides it, or writes its own.

steps.title: Call it from CI
steps.why: CI runs the same names on its runners. It needs Docker, Task and nothing project-specific.
actions: Make sure your runners can start containers. Docker-in-docker is fine, with capabilities dropped.
Install Task in the job, or use a small adapter that does it for you.
Call `task <name>` for each check. Decide in the workflow which events run which names.

code.label: The same call, different CIs
code.code:
# GitHub Actions
- run: task ci/node/build

# GitLab CI
script: task ci/node/build

# Jenkins
sh 'task ci/node/build'

steps.check: A pull request runs the same `ci/node/build` as your laptop and gets the same result.

steps.title: Gate the delivery
steps.why: Deploys need production keys. They run only in CI, after the checks, and skip the task wrapper.
actions: Add a final job that passes only when every check passed.
Run delivery after it, on tags or the main branch, with short-lived keys.
Keep delivery out of Taskfiles. Nobody should be able to deploy from a laptop.

zones.label: Reproducible tasks run anywhere. Privileged delivery runs only in CI.
zones.note: deploy is a right, not a command.

steps.check: Your laptop can run every `ci/*` task and none of the delivery steps.

finePrint.title: The fine print, in large type.
body: Pin versions on purpose. And know what the box promises, and what it doesn't.

pinned.title: Pinned on purpose
items: Images: a tag, or a digest for strict runs

same.label: Same
same.text: commands, image, mounts, env and cache rules

differ.label: May differ
differ.text: sources, CPU architecture, host kernel, credentials, network, cache contents

mine.title: One way to build it: mine.
body: My version is built for my stack and for GitHub. Use it as it is, or read it as an example for yours. The process doesn't mind.

projects.name: Images
projects.summary: Images for the stacks I use: Go, Rust, Python, Node, Nix and Terraform. Rebuilt every week, never tagged latest.

projects.name: Tasks
projects.summary: A module per tool on top of one hardened Docker runner. Projects include them pinned to a commit.

projects.name: Actions
projects.summary: task-run calls a task by name. Checks, a gate and delivery steps cover the rest. Built for GitHub.

projects.name: This site
projects.summary: This very page shipped through it: a Taskfile with ci/node/build and a few workflows that call it.

finale.title: Use these parts. Or build your own.
finale.body: Either way, you end up with one command, the same box everywhere, and a gate in front of production.
checklist: a shared Taskfile that runs them
a CI that calls the names
a gate in front of delivery
